resident.chief_complaint: Squeezing feeling at the midsection and tingling sensations in both upper and lower extremities.
resident.history: The patient is a 49-year-old male. Symptoms started approximately three months prior to the initial visit with a squeezing feeling at the midsection and tingling sensations in both upper and lower extremities. He reported no difficulty in walking. He demonstrated Lhermitte's sign when extending the neck abruptly. He denied any sensory and motor change. A diagnosis of ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL) of the cervical spine had been made before hospital admission.
resident.physical_exam: The patient denied any sensory and motor change on physical examination. Lhermitte's sign was elicited on abrupt neck extension. Motor power and reflexes are not documented.
key_positive_signs: Lhermitte's sign on abrupt neck extension
resident.past_history: Diagnosis of ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL) of the cervical spine was made before hospital admission. No other past medical history is documented.
resident.public_message: This 49-year-old male presented with a squeezing feeling at the midsection and tingling in both upper and lower extremities, symptoms beginning about three months before presentation. He had no difficulty walking. The patient denied any sensory and motor change on physical examination; however, Lhermitte's sign was elicited on abrupt neck extension. Imaging showed OPLL from C2 to C5 with atlas hypoplasia, spinal canal stenosis from C1 to C5 with cord compression at the atlas ring and an intramedullary high signal intensity area. Preoperative JOA score was 15 points.

imaging.public_message: I have not seen the films and am reporting only the case record's imaging description: OPLL was described from C2 through C5, with spinal canal stenosis from C1 through C5 and especially marked canal narrowing with cord compression at the atlas ring. An intramedullary high-signal area was reported. The record does not specify compression direction or a graded stenosis severity. These findings correlate well with the reported Lhermitte sign and bilateral sensory symptoms.

neurology.localization: Cervical spinal cord, most likely at C1-2 (atlas ring) given the marked canal stenosis and cord compression. Lhermitte sign and bilateral upper and lower extremity tingling with truncal squeezing are consistent with cervical myelopathy involving the dorsal columns and possibly spinothalamic tracts. Motor and reflex findings are not documented, so precise long-tract involvement is inferred.

red_flags.finding: Motor power and reflexes are not documented; sensory examination reportedly normal despite subjective tingling.
red_flags.rationale: This is an examination gap, not evidence of an alternative cause. Lhermitte sign is a positive finding and imaging shows cord compression, so the absence of documented motor/reflex changes does not undermine the myelopathic localization.

red_flags.finding: Marked canal narrowing and cord compression at the atlas ring due to atlas hypoplasia, distinct from the OPLL at C2-C5.
red_flags.rationale: If surgical decompression is planned primarily for OPLL at C2-C5, the upper cervical compression at C1-2 may require additional or different surgical consideration. The cord compression at the atlas ring is part of the same cervical myelopathy but could change the operative approach.

neurology.public_message: Findings localize to the cervical spinal cord, most likely C1-2, with Lhermitte sign and bilateral sensory symptoms. Imaging shows cord compression at the atlas ring and intramedullary signal change, correlating well (high match). Red flags: (1) Motor power and reflexes are not documented—a coexisting limitation, not an alternative cause; (2) Atlas ring compression from hypoplasia may change the surgical plan if decompression targets only OPLL levels. No symptom-imaging mismatch.

anesthesia.public_message: The patient is classified as ASA II. The intraoperative mean arterial pressure target is 85 mmHg. Blood loss risk is assessed as moderate. Prone position tolerance is assessed as moderate. Extubation difficulty is unassessable because no airway assessment is documented in the record.

physiatrist_opening.proposed_duration: 3-6 months of structured conservative management with close neurological monitoring
preconditions_for_failure: Development of new objective motor weakness (MRC grade ≤4/5) or gait instability
Worsening of JOA score by ≥2 points from baseline of 15
Appearance of bladder or bowel dysfunction
Progression of intramedullary T2 hyperintensity or new cord compression on follow-up MRI
Persistent or worsening symptoms despite 6 months of conservative treatment
physiatrist_opening.public_message: I acknowledge the imaging demonstrates significant stenosis and cord signal change; however, the patient currently presents with mild symptoms (JOA 15, no motor or gait deficits documented, only subjective tingling and Lhermitte sign). A structured 3-6 month trial of conservative management—cervical isometric strengthening, posture education, avoidance of high-risk maneuvers, and close neurological surveillance—is a reasonable first step. Surgical decompression is indicated only if there is objective neurological deterioration (new motor weakness, gait decline, sphincter involvement) or worsening T2 signal on follow-up MRI. The success rate of observation and conservative therapy in mild myelopathy without obvious motor deficit is approximately 40%, and a trial can be undertaken safely with frequent reassessment.

physiatrist_final.public_message: The argument put to me is again the cord signal change at the atlas ring. I have already weighed this finding carefully: cord T2 signal change is a risk factor for progression, but in a patient with JOA 15, no documented motor or gait deficit, and only sensory symptoms and Lhermitte sign, it does not by itself prove that a brief, closely monitored conservative trial would be unsafe. The deputy director has not offered a reason why atlas-level signal change outweighs the absence of clinical myelopathy deficits. I hold my position pending completion of the requested examination and imaging; if progressive myelopathy is confirmed, I will reconsider.

vice_opinions.assessment: Imaging shows critical stenosis at C1 with cord compression and T2 cord signal change in a patient with clinical myelopathy (JOA 15, Lhermitte sign, band-like dysesthesia). Even though motor deficits are not documented, atlas-level compression and intramedullary signal change place him at high risk for progression. I favor surgical decompression rather than a conservative trial; the imaging severity outweighs the currently mild examination. However, the record lacks key data that should be obtained before final decision: formal motor power, reflexes (Hoffmann, clonus), spasticity, sphincter function, dynamic radiographs, CT to define OPLL morphology, and axial MRI to confirm compression direction and C1 canal dimensions.
proposed_options: Posterior decompression: C1 posterior arch resection + C2-C5 laminoplasty (e.g., open-door), with or without instrumented fusion depending on OPLL extent and dynamic stability.
Posterior decompression C1-C5 with instrumented fusion (C1 lateral mass fixation to C5 lateral mass/pedicle) if kyphosis, instability, or OPLL occupying >50% of canal is present.

If axial imaging shows dominant anterior OPLL compression with severe canal compromise, consider anterior decompression (corpectomy/OPLL resection), possibly combined with posterior approach; however, this is less suited to atlas-level compression.

Structured observation and conservative therapy with close neurological monitoring, reserved only if patient declines surgery or if additional workup shows no objective myelopathy; I do not favor this as the primary plan.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Posterior decompression: C1 posterior arch resection + C2-C5 laminoplasty, with fusion decided after CT and dynamic imaging; I would not delay for a conservative trial.
disagreement_points: I disagree with the physiatrist's recommendation to defer surgery for 3-6 months in the presence of atlas-level cord compression and T2 signal change; this risks irreversible progression.
The lack of documented motor power and reflexes is a data gap, not reassurance; JOA 15 with primarily sensory symptoms still represents myelopathy and cannot be treated as 'no objective deficit.'
If conservative management is to be considered, explicit surveillance triggers must be defined; otherwise the patient may be referred too late.
deferred_questions_to_director: Do you want preoperative CT and flexion-extension radiographs obtained before committing to decompression levels and fusion?
Given the atlas hypoplasia, should vertebral artery imaging (CTA) and C1 screw feasibility be assessed if fusion is planned?
If axial imaging shows >50% OPLL canal occupancy with anterior compression, would you consider anterior decompression or a combined approach?

I would plan C1 posterior arch resection and C2-C5 laminoplasty, with fusion depending on CT and dynamic stability. I recommend obtaining motor/reflex exam, CT, and flexion-extension films before finalizing.

vice_opinions.assessment: I agree surgery is indicated, and I support the director's decision to obtain missing examination and imaging data before finalizing the approach. My working plan is posterior decompression to address both the atlas ring stenosis and the C2-C5 OPLL. C1 posterior arch resection is necessary for the atlas-level cord compression, and C2-C5 laminoplasty covers the OPLL segments. I would add fusion only if CT or flexion-extension views demonstrate instability or unacceptable kyphosis risk. The mild clinical presentation does not outweigh the C1 cord signal change, so I do not favor a prolonged conservative trial.
proposed_options: Posterior decompression with C1 posterior arch resection and C2-C5 laminoplasty, adding instrumented fusion only if dynamic instability or post-laminectomy kyphosis risk is demonstrated.
Anterior or combined anterior-posterior decompression if axial CT shows severe focal anterior OPLL occupancy and/or kyphotic alignment that would compromise posterior decompression.
Short monitored conservative trial with repeat MRI and clinical reassessment at 3 months, which I would not recommend given the atlas-level cord signal change.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Posterior decompression with C1 posterior arch resection and C2-C5 laminoplasty, adding fusion only for demonstrated instability or significant kyphosis risk.
disagreement_points: Whether the mild clinical deficit and JOA 15 can justify any conservative trial, given the atlas-level cord signal change; I do not believe it does.
Whether C1 posterior arch resection alone sufficiently decompresses the atlas ring or must be extended to C2-C5 laminoplasty; I favor the latter because OPLL and stenosis extend to C5.
The threshold for adding fusion: I would avoid routine fusion, but atlas hypoplasia and OPLL may create craniocervical or subaxial instability that CT/dynamic films must answer.
I question whether anterior/combined approach is truly mandated solely by >50% OPLL occupancy; in diffuse OPLL without kyphosis, posterior decompression usually suffices.
deferred_questions_to_director: After CT and dynamic imaging, do you wish to make the final posterior versus anterior/combined decision yourself at reconvene, or may I proceed with a posterior plan if CT shows no severe focal anterior mass?
Should we tentatively schedule surgery while tests are pending, or wait for all data before booking?
